author: Mavic Conde
title: UN raises standard for IP consent
content:
Photo courtesy of Marcelino Tena

“This is reasonable, provided that what the guidance says is followed in practice.”

The United Nations stressed this point in its new guidance on the free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) for business projects affecting Indigenous Peoples territories.

The guidance, issued by the UN Human Rights Council in June, states that governments should seek and obtain FPIC before granting licenses or concessions within ancestral domains. They must also ensure that Indigenous Peoples’ rights are respected, including when decisions need a longer time or a reassessment.

It stresses that consent is “not a one-time event but an ongoing process.” According to the report, Indigenous Peoples have the right to reconsider their decisions if circumstances change, agreed conditions are not fulfilled, or new information emerges about the project’s impact. They may also decline to participate if they believe consultations are not being conducted in good faith or need more time and resources to strengthen their institutions.

The guidance addresses recurring concerns of governments conducting consultations only after having granted key approvals and failure to recognize that consent is “dynamic and iterative in nature.”

These gaps in implementation have “caused conflicts, resulted in harm, and triggered cycles of violence confronting States and businesses with Indigenous Peoples,” the report said.

“I believe this is reasonable, provided that what the guidance says is followed in practice.” Marcelino Tena, a Dumagat-Remontado Indigenous leader, said in Filipino in a virtual interview with Bulatlat.

Tena was among those who challenged the consultation process for the Kaliwa Dam project in Quezon and Rizal provinces, arguing that it failed to reflect community opposition and adequately represent their decisions.

The UN guidance came a month after the Philippine National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) approved the revised 2012 FPIC guidelines. Recognized under the 1997 Indigenous Peoples Rights Act and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), FPIC is intended to ensure that Indigenous communities can make informed decisions about projects affecting their territories.

The revised guidelines classify projects into Category A, B, and C, with different consent procedures. Categories A and B require FPIC through customary decision-making processes while Category C projects such as community-driven, non-commercial, and many government-funded projects may proceed with a shortened validation instead of the full procedure.

The changes have drawn criticism from human rights advocates, including the Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center (LRC). In a briefer, the non-profit cultural research organization described the 2026 framework a critical departure from the 2012 guidelines, stressing that it “strips away the vital safeguard of community oversight.”

“Characterizing [redacted] projects as Category C merely because they are government-funded and non-commercial fails to account for their actual impacts on Indigenous communities and their ancestral domains,” the LRC said.

The organization warned that compressed timelines could affect meaningful participation, as internal consultations take time and attending meetings often requires days of travel on foot.

In a statement, the Human Rights Watch said that while the declaration is not a binding treaty, the Philippines supported its adoption by the UN General Assembly in 2007.

The NCIP initially acknowledged Bulatlat’s request for comment but has not yet provided a response.

Tena said that his community completed and submitted its Ancestral Domain Sustainable Development and Protection Plan (ADSDPP) to the NCIP in September. The plan guides the protection and governance of their ancestral domain under customary laws. He said that the plan and their certificate of ancestral land domain title (CADT) cannot exist without the other. The community obtained its CADT in 2008 but developing the plan took nearly two decades.

In a Facebook post, Tena acknowledged disagreements during the process which he said were necessary to identify and support the community’s collective will.

The Philippines is among the countries the UN Working Group cited as having laws requiring consultation with IPs. But the report warns that legal recognition alone does not guarantee effective implementation of the FPIC. For companies and investors, the guidance states taht responsibility does not end with complying with national laws, for Indigenous rights should be respected even when communities do not have formal government recognition or land titles. (DAA)

title: Farmers, fisherfolk demand urgent aid amid El Niño, rising fuel prices
content:
The absence of reliable irrigation makes it difficult for farmers to continue planting during periods of extreme heat.







By Wendyl Geronimo

Davao Today




From drought-stricken farms in Davao and Nueva Ecija to fishing communities in Albay, farmers and fisherfolk are demanding government assistance, protection against land grabbing and genuine agrarian reform as El Niño, mounting production costs and development projects threaten their livelihoods.




Amid worsening agricultural conditions, rising production expenses and continuing disputes over land ownership, farmers and fisherfolk across the Philippines are calling for immediate government intervention, warning that insufficient assistance and threats of displacement are pushing rural communities deeper into poverty.




Their demands come as agricultural communities confront the effects of El Niño, inadequate irrigation systems, expensive fuel and fertilizer, and development projects that farmers organizations say threaten thousands of hectares of farmland.




In the Davao Region, prolonged dry conditions have affected agricultural production, particularly among farmers dependent on rainfall.




Approximately P410 million in agricultural losses were recorded in the Davao region due to El Niño.

title: Thousands of farmlands in Bicol converted to mining, energy, infra projects
content:
Claiming the Land: Kilusang Magbubukid ng Bicol provides assistance to affected farmers and members of the local peasant group in Bula, Camarines Sur. (Photo By Reynard Magtoto/Bulatlat)

Farmers organizations warned that agricultural land conversion and large-scale development projects could displace farming communities, threaten food production and undermine farmers’ access to land.

Farmers organizations in the Bicol region have raised concerns over alleged land grabbing and agricultural land conversion involving haciendas, mining operations, renewable energy developments and infrastructure projects.

The farmers travelled to Manila late in October to call on the Marcos Jr. administration to stop land grabbing and land-use conversion of agricultural lands.

In Camarines Norte, peasant groups identified 25,000 hectares associated with the Mabilo Copper-Gold Project, while another 64,884 hectares were linked to a renewable energy development in Mount Labo.

An additional 321 hectares were identified in connection with mining operations in the province.

In Albay, the organizations identified several disputed landholdings, including 141 hectares at Hacienda Mitra/Illas in Guinobatan, 130 hectares at Hacienda Alsua in Pio Duran, 250 hectares at Hacienda Asistio in Ligao, and 200 hectares at Hacienda Ribaya, also in Ligao.

Another 78 hectares were identified at a Hacienda Alsua

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Hegseth visit exposes deepening US military intervention in the Philippines
content:
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth attends a meeting in Cebu on October 28, 2026, together with other defense leaders from other countries. Photo from the Department of National Defense's Facebook page

For ILPS Philippines, these agreements are not merely defense arrangements. They further integrate the country into Washington’s military operations and its First Island Chain strategy against China.

The arrival of US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in Cebu on October 28 has drawn condemnation from progressive groups, which warned that the Philippines is increasingly being drawn into Washington’s military and economic agenda at the expense of national sovereignty.

The International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines said Hegseth’s visit for the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting comes amid the Trump administration’s aggressive expansion of US military power in the Asia-Pacific and its preparations for greater confrontation with China.

The group described Hegseth as a key enforcer of Washington’s war agenda, criticizing Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration for facilitating the growing US military presence in the country.

Under the Marcos administration, military cooperation between Manila and Washington has expanded through weapons deployments, joint military exercises, intelligence-sharing arrangements, and the increased use of Philippine military facilities.

Read: Missiles, markets, and massacres: Balikatan, ASEAN, and the war logic of US imperial decline*

During Hegseth’s March 2025 visit, the two governments agreed to deploy advanced US weapons, including the Navy Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS), expand high-end military exercises, strengthen defense-industrial cooperation, and launch joint cyber operations.

In October 2025, Hegseth and Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. announced a Task Force-Philippines to strengthen joint military planning and operational coordination. This was followed by a 15-year Communications Interoperability and Security Memorandum of Agreement (CISMOA) in May 2026, further institutionalizing secure military communications and information-sharing between the two countries.

These arrangements build on the General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA) and the nine Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) sites across the Philippines.

For ILPS Philippines, these agreements are not merely defense arrangements. They further integrate the country into Washington’s military operations and its First Island Chain strategy against China.

The consequences, the group warned, extend beyond military installations. With US forces increasingly capable of operating advanced weapons from Philippine territory, Filipino communities could become vulnerable to retaliation in the event of a regional conflict.

Read: Tacloban fishers slam Balikatan exercises

During the May 2026 Balikatan exercises, the US military reportedly launched a Tomahawk cruise missile from Tacloban Airport, demonstrating its capacity to conduct long-range missile strikes from Philippine soil.

“Our country is being transformed into a forward operating platform for US wars, exposing millions of Filipinos to the grave danger of retaliation, devastation, and death in a regional conflict,” ILPS Philippines said.

The group accused the Marcos administration of sacrificing national independence through its cooperation with Washington, using tensions with China to justify the expanding US military footprint.

While opposing China’s coercion and violations of Philippine sovereign rights, ILPS Philippines stressed that the country cannot defend its sovereignty by allowing another foreign power to use its territory for military operations and war preparations.

Progressive groups also warned that US intervention is not confined to military installations. They said Washington’s economic initiatives are tied to its strategic interests in the Philippines, particularly its access to critical resources and supply chains.

The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) condemned Hegseth’s visit, saying the US is pursuing both military access and greater control over resources through initiatives such as Pax Silica.

A US-led initiative seeking to secure supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, and other strategic technologies, Pax Silica could further open Philippine resources to foreign corporate interests, the farmers’ group warned.

KMP Chairperson Danilo Ramos said the Marcos administration is surrendering the country’s sovereignty on both military and economic fronts.

“Washington wants access not only to our territory for its war machine but also to our resources. Farmers and rural communities will bear the cost through land grabbing, resource extraction and displacement,” Ramos said.

The group linked these concerns to the Luzon Economic Corridor, which includes infrastructure and industrial projects that could support US strategic and commercial interests.

Among the developments cited were shipyard expansion in Subic for US military warships, an ammunition hub, and a proposed advanced manufacturing park in Capas, Tarlac, intended to support artificial intelligence supply chains.

KMP warned that these projects could intensify pressure on agricultural and ancestral lands, further threatening farmers already struggling with landlessness, agricultural imports, and the encroachment of mining and large-scale energy projects.

For rural communities, the group said, the consequences could mean displacement, loss of livelihood, and greater foreign corporate control over the country’s natural resources.

“Marcos is selling out our sovereignty on both military and economic fronts,” Ramos said.

Meanwhile, the Makabayan coalition demanded transparency over the latest military arrangements, including their financial implications, operational scope, and consequences for national security.

The growing US military presence has also raised questions about Washington’s own record of military operations and accountability.

Hegseth has faced scrutiny from US lawmakers over strikes on suspected drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean, including reports of a follow-up strike that killed survivors. Lawmakers have likewise raised concerns over alleged violations of the laws of armed conflict involving civilian casualties in Iran, including the bombing of a girls’ school in Minab.

Ramos said such incidents must be investigated and those responsible held accountable.

“Deliberately killing defenseless survivors and unlawfully attacking civilians are grave violations of international humanitarian law. US officials like Hegseth must be held accountable, not shielded by their political and military power,” he said.

For progressive groups, the issue goes beyond Hegseth’s visit. It reflects the continuing struggle against foreign intervention and the country’s dependence on a military power whose geopolitical interests do not necessarily serve the Filipino people.

ILPS Philippines stressed that opposing US intervention does not mean tolerating aggression by China or any other foreign power. Rather, genuine sovereignty means refusing to surrender Philippine territory, resources, and military facilities to foreign strategic ambitions.

“The region needs genuine peace, not more American missiles, military bases, and troops,” the group said.

KMP called on Filipinos to oppose US intervention and demand the termination of unequal military agreements that facilitate Washington’s military presence and operations in the country.

“We must fight for genuine independence, national sovereignty and freedom,” Ramos said. (AMU, RVO)

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: 9 years later, parents still seek answers over son’s killing amid ‘drug war’
content:
Nanette Castillo, mother of a drug war victim, expresses her sentiment during a protest at the University of the Philippines Diliman on February 27, 2026, in conjunction with the last day of Rodrigo Duterte's confirmation of charges hearing before the International Criminal Court. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat

Nine years later, the family still has no definitive answers about who killed their son, why the gunmen targeted him, and whether authorities thoroughly investigated the shooting.

Trigger warning: details of violence and death

Nine years after their son was killed in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Nanette and Bong Castillo stepped forward to the Truth Commission’s fifth Public Truth-Telling Session on October 23 to recount what they believe happened to Aldrin Castillo and seek answers on his death.

They believe that the case of their son may have been a case of mistaken-identity, while the police and medical records reviewed by forensic pathologist Raquel Fortun exposed significant gaps in the original documentation of Aldrin’s death.

Aldrin was 32 when gunmen shot him in Tondo, Manila, on October 2, 2017. He was visiting his sister to help repair her air conditioner.

His parents believe the gunmen were looking for another man and killed Aldrin because they mistook him for their intended target.

Nine years later, the family still has no definitive answers about who killed their son, why the gunmen targeted him, and whether authorities thoroughly investigated the shooting.

Nanette came to the Truth Commission determined to tell people who Aldrin was beyond the circumstances of his death.

“I want everyone to know how good Aldrin was as a son,” she said in Filipino.

Aldrin was her firstborn, whom she remembered as affectionate, hardworking, and attentive to the needs of others.

In elementary school, he was recognized for keeping himself neat and clean, and he ranked first in his class in Grade 4.

Nanette recalled that he would ask her to share food with friends who had nothing to eat, even when their own family had little money.

When Aldrin began earning, he gave his mother part of his salary and made sure they ate together before she went home.

Bong also brought his son to catering jobs so he could learn to work and earn money.

Aldrin later learned welding through his partner’s family and dreamed of working abroad to give his parents a better life.

Nanette remembered his promise to take her to Saudi Arabia and build her a house when he found work there.

“Gagawin kitang doña,” (I will make you rich.) Aldrin would tell her.

For Nanette, the promise represented a future her son wanted to build for their family, a future cut short when he was killed.

On October 2, 2017, Aldrin visited his sister in Tondo to help repair her air conditioner.

Nanette hesitated before allowing him to leave because she had heard reports of killings in the area. She thought the checkpoints and the election gun ban in effect at the time might help keep him safe.

She gave him money for transportation and watched him leave.

Bong was away in Quezon City for work when the family learned that Aldrin had been shot.

According to the police incident report presented by Fortun, Aldrin was with friends in Tondo when armed men arrived on motorcycles and shot him before fleeing.

Nanette recalled reaching the scene and finding her son lying motionless on the street, his eyes open.

She called for a doctor and an ambulance, still hoping someone could save him.

She held his hand and pressed her ear against his chest, trying to feel a pulse or hear a heartbeat.

“Umaasa ako. Umaasa ako. Umaasa ako,” she recalled, repeating how she kept hoping that her son might still be alive.

Nanette also recounted how police officers initially prevented her from approaching Aldrin, saying she might disturb the crime scene. She pleaded to stay beside him, promising not to move anything.

The shock of that night has remained with her.

She still remembers the ordinary details of life with Aldrin, including the meals he loved and the way he would come home and ask what they would eat.

Those memories now coexist with the questions that followed his death.

During the session, Nanette recalled hearing that the gunmen had been looking for someone wearing a white sleeveless shirt. It was her nephew who mentioned this detail.

Bong also recounted that a man later approached him and said he was the person the gunmen had been looking for that night.

The parents presented these accounts as the basis for their belief that Aldrin was killed by mistake.

Their account has not, in the material presented during the session, established the identity of the intended target or the people responsible for the shooting.

The possibility of mistaken identity has nevertheless shaped the family’s search for answers. If the gunmen were looking for someone else, the family wants to know why Aldrin was killed and who was behind the attack.

Nanette continues to ask people in the area, including tricycle drivers, whether they know anything about the killing.

She said she returns to the place where Aldrin fell to light candles and ask questions, hoping someone might share information that could help clarify what happened.

“Parang hanggang ngayon nga po ako’y nag-iimbestiga,” she said, describing how she still finds herself investigating her son’s death.

Her words underscored a central concern raised by the case: the burden of seeking answers has continued to fall on the family, even years after the killing.

Raquel Fortun reviewed Aldrin’s death certificate, police autopsy report, incident report, and crime-scene photographs. She also examined his remains after they were exhumed on September 24, 2026, with the family’s consent.

Her presentation identified significant shortcomings in the documentation of Aldrin’s death and the subsequent investigation.

Fortun first questioned the death certificate’s incomplete manner-of-death field. She said it should have identified the death as homicide rather than leaving the field blank.

She also criticized the record’s reference to “death by legal intervention,” questioning the terminology used.

The police autopsy report, conducted on October 3, 2017, the day after Aldrin was shot, stated that he had sustained five through-and-through gunshot wounds. Fortun noted that the body had already been embalmed before the examination.

She said the report was only about one and a half pages long and lacked the detail needed to document the injuries adequately.

The report described gunshot wounds to the head, neck, and trunk, including injuries involving the spinal cord, a major blood vessel, the lungs, heart, liver, and intestines.

But Fortun questioned whether the report sufficiently documented the injuries and their trajectories. Without a detailed account of the entry and exit wounds, she said, it was difficult to determine which wounds corresponded to one another.

The limitations of the original autopsy became particularly important years later, when Fortun examined the preserved remains.

During the September exhumation, she examined the bones and conducted X-rays. Her preliminary findings identified fractures consistent with gunfire to the head and neck region and the trunk, including damage to the first cervical vertebra and ribs.

However, the remains could not answer every question. The soft tissue had decomposed, and the passage of years limited what could be determined from the bones alone.

Fortun said she could only assess the evidence available to her. She also expressed hope that additional records and materials could be obtained to clarify the case.

Her presentation did not identify the gunmen or establish who ordered the killing. Instead, it highlighted the limitations of the original medical documentation and the questions that remain because the available evidence does not provide a complete reconstruction of the shooting.

Raquel Fortun’s concerns extended beyond the autopsy to the police investigation at the crime scene.

The police incident report described men arriving on motorcycles before shooting Aldrin and fleeing. Investigators recovered five spent cartridge casings, according to the records Fortun presented: two .45-caliber casings and three .40-caliber casings.

But the available documentation did not provide a complete account of the shooting or establish what further investigative steps had been taken.

Fortun questioned the handling and documentation of evidence at the scene, pointing to photographs that raised concerns about crime-scene control, lighting, and the way evidence was marked.

She also raised questions about whether investigators had adequately documented physical evidence and followed up on potential leads.

The gaps in the records left Fortun unable to reconstruct the attack with greater certainty. She said the original investigators should have gathered and documented evidence more thoroughly.

“The people who should have done the investigation, the gathering of evidence, the documentation should have done their job,” she said.

Fortun acknowledged the limits of what the Truth Commission could establish from the available material. Without more evidence, she said, the Commission could not confidently determine what further action the case might warrant.

The shortcomings she identified do not establish who killed Aldrin or prove the family’s mistaken-identity theory. They do, however, raise questions about the completeness of the investigation and whether authorities did enough to establish the circumstances of his death.

Aldrin’s death fractured the Castillo family in ways that extended far beyond the funeral.

Nanette said she blamed herself for allowing him to go to Tondo and later blamed her daughter for asking her brother to visit.

She stopped speaking to her daughter for more than a year because she could not understand why the family had lost Aldrin.

Bong described trying to support his wife while dealing with his own grief and anger.

He said he sometimes withdrew or drank to cope, while Nanette struggled with the emptiness of returning home without her son.

Their pain also followed them online, where strangers mocked Aldrin and told the family that he deserved to die because they believed he was involved with drugs.

Nanette said she initially fought back against such comments, but she later learned to ignore people who did not know her son or understand what the family had endured.

“Kung hindi niyo kami kayang damayan, huwag niyo kaming bastusin,” she said, asking people not to insult the family if they could not offer support.

She told the commission that even if people accused someone of a crime, they should not celebrate that person’s death.

The family’s account challenged narratives that reduce people killed during the drug war to labels that make their deaths appear acceptable.

Nanette said she wanted the public to know Aldrin as a son, brother, worker, and person with plans for his future.

The Castillo family wants those responsible for Aldrin’s killing to be identified and held accountable.

Bong thanked the Truth Commission for giving them an opportunity to tell their story. Nanette said she hoped the Commission would help establish what happened to her son.

She called on those responsible for the killing, whether police officers or people paid to carry out the drug war, to confront the harm they had caused.

Nanette said she would not seek revenge. She wanted those responsible to face due process, the protection that Aldrin did not receive before gunmen shot him.

For the family, accountability would not bring Aldrin back. But establishing the truth could help them understand his death and prevent other families from experiencing the same loss.

Fortun’s presentation showed how incomplete records and unanswered investigative questions can constrain efforts to establish the circumstances of a killing years later.

The Commission’s next steps will depend in part on whether additional records and evidence can be obtained to clarify the gaps Fortun identified.

At the end of the session, participants took part in a ritual for loved ones who had died, represented by an empty chair and a lit candle.

Nanette read a poem she had written for Aldrin, recalling the difficulty of saying goodbye to a son whose absence continues to shape her life.

She remembered his familiar questions about dinner and the sound of his voice at home.

“Walang hanggang pagmamahal, Aldrin ko, hanggang sa muli nating pagkikita, anak,” she said, ending the poem with a promise of enduring love.

Nine years after Aldrin’s killing, his parents gave their account before the Truth Commission and renewed their call for answers.

Their testimony has brought the case back into public view, while Fortun’s review has highlighted the limitations of the records left behind. Who killed Aldrin, whether he was mistaken for someone else, and whether the remaining evidence can help establish accountability are questions that still await answers. (RTS, RVO)

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: SC ruling exposes pork barrel system
content:
Photo by Supreme Court of the Philippines

A significant part of the ruling concerned the Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP).

The Supreme Court’s (SC) declaration that the 2024 and 2025 national budgets were unconstitutional has renewed calls to hold Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and other government officials accountable for the flood control corruption scandal. This also exposes how budget insertions and discretionary funds enabled the questionable use of billions of pesos in public money.

In its October 7 ruling on Lagman v. Congress (G.R. No. 271059), the high court struck down budgetary additions that exceeded the spending ceiling submitted by the President. It also permanently prohibited the release mechanisms for certain Unprogrammed Appropriations (UA) under the 2026 national budget.

For progressive lawmakers, the decision affirms long-standing warnings that the pork barrel system persisted despite earlier Supreme Court (SC) rulings restricting discretionary and lump-sum appropriations.

“The party’s over,” said ACT Teachers Partylist Rep. Antonio Tinio, deputy minority leader, in his October 21 discussion of the ruling.

Tinio said that the decision exposed how Congress and Malacañang used budgetary mechanisms to expand allocations beyond the limits set by the executive’s proposed budget, creating opportunities for patronage and corruption.

The court ruled that the national budget ceiling covers both programmed and unprogrammed appropriations. Congress cannot increase their combined total beyond the amount submitted by the President.

In the 2024 budget, lawmakers added P449.5 billion ($7.02 Billion) to unprogrammed appropriations. In 2025, they added P17.99 billion ($208.83 Million) to the Department of Public Works and Highways’ (DPWH) Special Road Fund. The court declared these additions unconstitutional and, consequently, the respective General Appropriations Acts.

The ruling also found that certain release conditions for unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 budget violated constitutional requirements. The provisions allowed the executive to determine which projects would receive funding without clear standards for prioritization.

A significant part of the ruling concerned the Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP), which the court declared unconstitutional as a prohibited lump-sum appropriation.

According to Tinio, P200 billion ($3.12 Billion) was released through SAGIP in 2024. Of this amount, P155.9 billion ($2.43 Billion) went to the DPWH during the final quarter of the year, including P85.8 billion ($1.34 Billion) for flood control projects.

The court described SAGIP as a covert repository for lump-sum allocations for DPWH infrastructure projects, including flood control.

The arrangement allowed the executive to determine the projects and amounts to be funded after Congress passed the budget, undermining legislative oversight over public spending.

The court also cited economist Solita Monsod’s observation that discretionary DPWH allocations had become a new form of pork barrel, reportedly accompanied by a six-percent “parking fee.”

The ruling criticized congressional amendments that reduced funding for strategic development projects while increasing allocations for infrastructure and assistance programs that could be used for political patronage.

Among the projects affected by cuts in the 2024 budget were the North-South Commuter Railway which faced a P53.93 billion ($841.87 Million) shortfall, and the Metro Manila Subway which faced a P52.63 billion ($821.57 Million) shortfall.

The court said that Congress created artificial fiscal space by reducing funding for development programs and redirecting allocations to other budget items, including DPWH infrastructure and assistance programs under the Department of Health, Department of Social Welfare and Development, and Department of Labor and Employment.

According to Makabayan, these findings highlight how budget decisions can deprive essential public services of funding while expanding discretionary spending that lacks sufficient transparency.

For the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), the ruling vindicated progressive lawmakers who opposed the 2024 and 2025 national budgets, warning that the flood control scandal demonstrated the consequences of allowing pork barrel allocations to persist.

During the ratification of the bicameral conference committee reports for both budgets, the only House members who voted against them were France Castro of ACT Teachers Party-list, Arlene Brosas of Gabriela Women’s Party, and Raoul Manuel of Kabataan Party-list.

The three opposed the 2024 budget over its massive unprogrammed appropriations, confidential and intelligence funds, and inadequate funding for social services and public utilities.

They again voted against the 2025 budget, citing the sudden expansion of unprogrammed appropriations, the lack of transparency in bicameral insertions, and cuts to essential sectors such as education and health.

Bayan President Renato Reyes Jr. said that the SC affirmed concerns repeatedly raised by Makabayan legislators, progressive organizations, and anti-corruption advocates about the expansion of pork barrel funds and infrastructure insertions.

He accused Marcos Jr. of playing a central role in the system that allowed questionable allocations to proliferate, calling for him to face investigation and prosecution over his alleged role in the flood control scandal.

The allegations against individual officials must still be established through appropriate investigations and legal proceedings.

The SC criticized the bicameral conference committee for failing to adequately explain its changes to the national budget. During the proceedings, Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa asked for documents showing which programs had been cut and which had received additional funding. The solicitor general reportedly replied that “there are really no documents.”

The high court stressed that the bicameral conference committee does not have unlimited authority to rewrite the budget. Its mandate is confined to reconciling provisions on which the House and Senate disagree, and the ratification of its report cannot cure constitutional violations.

For Tinio, the ruling also raises questions about the liability of those who authored, proposed, and implemented the unconstitutional appropriations.

The court clarified that the doctrine of operative fact would apply only to projects that could no longer be undone and beneficiaries who acted in good faith. It did not automatically exempt the authors, proponents, and implementers from criminal, civil, or administrative liability, subject to the findings of the proper tribunal.

Tinio urged the Office of the Ombudsman and the Commission on Audit to examine the liability of officials involved in the questioned allocations.

He said that the ruling strengthened the impeachment complaint endorsed by the Makabayan bloc against Marcos Jr. in January in connection with the flood control scandal, particularly the allegations concerning his role in approving projects funded through unprogrammed appropriations.

The ruling comes as Congress deliberates on the proposed 2027 national budget where Tinio warned that several provisions appear to repeat mechanisms that the SC already invalidated or restricted.

These include release conditions for unprogrammed appropriations similar to those permanently prohibited under the 2026 budget, as well as a P42.55 billion ($664.22 Million) allocation for foreign-assisted projects without an itemized list of projects, loans, or implementing agencies.

Tinio also questioned proposed lump-sum allocations and congressional amendments that increased funding for selected programs while reducing allocations for foreign-assisted projects. He warned that the proposed budget could face further constitutional challenges if these provisions remain unchanged.

He called on the House of Representatives to reconsider its proposed budget and release a complete report explaining the amendments. He also urged the Senate to remove prohibited lump sums, correct the release conditions for unprogrammed appropriations, and restore funding for essential public services.

Reyes, meanwhile, called on the people to remain vigilant throughout the Senate and bicameral budget deliberations, stressing that the ruling should guide efforts to remove pork barrel allocations and redirect public funds toward social services.

Earlier Supreme Court rulings, including Belgica v. Ochoa and Araullo v. Aquino, had already established restrictions on pork barrel and unconstitutional fund releases. Yet the flood control scandal revealed how questionable practices could persist through new budgetary mechanisms.

Reyes warned that corruption would continue to find ways to survive unless the public challenged the patronage system underpinning the national budget.

For the petitioners and progressive lawmakers like Makabayan who opposed the questioned appropriations, the ruling is a victory. But the fight is far from over: the public must still demand that those responsible be held accountable and that the national budget prioritize the needs of ordinary Filipinos over political interests. (AMU, DAA)

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Cyberlibel complaints vs journalists strengthen calls to decriminalize libel
content:
The criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Libel complaints were recently filed against journalists and media company executives. For a journalists’ group, these validate the previous calls to decriminalize libel.

The GMA chapter of the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) stressed that libel laws silence journalism. “[C]riminalizing speech only undermines the public’s fundamental right to know,” the chapter said in a statement.

Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte filed libel and cyberlibel complaints against GMA executives and broadcast journalists which stemmed from the network’s report about alleged cash deliveries to the Dutertes claimed by dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Duterte filed the complaint before the Davao City Prosecutor’s Office on October 23, more than two weeks after his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, made a joke about filing a multimillion-peso libel case against GMA Network. Her remarks happened during a press conference on October 6 while reading her affidavit which answers Gracioso’s claims.

Among the respondents were GMA executives Felipe Gozon and Gilberto Duavit, as well as journalists Mel Tiangco, Vicki Morales, Emil Sumangil, Darlene Cay, Marvin Parado, Joel San Luis, and other unidentified individuals.

In a statement released on October 23, the TV network said that they have not yet received the complaints.

Gracioso and National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) director Melvin Matibag were also named as respondents.

Meanwhile, veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on October 24 over a cyberlibel complaint reportedly filed by Mans Carpio, Sara’s husband. He was unaware of the complaint, according to his legal counsel. He was released on bail on the same day.

NUJP has been campaigning for the decriminalization of libel, echoing the views of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Committee that the criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Right(s) Up: Why journalists and advocates push for decriminalization of libel

On September 18, NUJP released its policy review on libel laws, stating that the high court has already identified the problem of these laws but reform requires legislation. The review, to name a few, cited Justice Marvic Leonen’s opinion in Disini, Jr. v. Secretary of Justice which stated that libel was unconstitutional as penal sanctions impose “an invidious chilling effect.”

It added that removing jail time alone, as proposed by some legislators, is not decriminalization because of limitations of a fine-only regime, saying that if the accused cannot pay, subsidiary imprisonment may follow.

The review cited the data obtained from the Office of Cybercrime of the Department of Justice (DOJ), indicating that 3,770 cyberlibel cases had been filed, as of May 2022, since the enactment of the Cybercrime Prevention Act. More than 2,500 cases remained pending in courts and before the prosecution level. There were already 12 convictions.

In the 2023 study by NUJP, 61.5% of the libel cases against 50 journalists from 2021 to 2023 were filed by politicians.

ML Party-list Rep. Leila de Lima said that filing a libel suit against journalists and media workers for doing their job sends a “chilling message” to other members of the press. Parties being accused can just respond to the allegations, she wrote in a Facebook post.

Under the Journalist’s Code of Ethics approved by media groups, journalists shall recognize the duty to air the other side and the duty to correct substantive errors promptly.

“Contrary to allegations of malice or unverified reporting, the report went through standard, multi-layered editorial and legal verification procedures,” the NUJP GMA Chapter said. “The team conducted due diligence—verifying information through official sources, law enforcement documents, and background checks—and obtained proper clearance from network leadership and legal counsel before airing the story.”

In the subject report, the reporter, Cay, and anchor Tiangco mentioned that they were trying to get the comments of the people implicated by Gracioso, including the Dutertes, but they did not receive a response when the report was aired last month.

Prior to the complaints filed against GMA executives and news personalities and Lustre, NUJP documented 16 incidents involving filing libel and cyberlibel against the media under the Marcos Jr. administration. (DAA)

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Proposed foreign-funded wind projects threaten Bicol fishers
content:
Photo frrom Province of Camarines Sur

“If they say this project is for development, development for whom? This is not for us fisherfolk.”

Norberto Tobias of Tanggol San Miguel Bay (SMB) Network stressed this point as he and other fisherfolk from Bicol expressed opposition to the planned 1,000-megawatt San Miguel Bay Offshore Wind Farm.

They joined the Kampuhang Magbubukid (peasant camp) in front of the Department of Agrarian Reform from October 15 to 20.

The proposed wind farm covers 23,307 hectares of coastal waters across municipalities in Camarines Sur and Camarines Norte, including the fishing communities in Calabanga, Cabusao, Tinambac, Siruma, Sipocot, Basud, and Mercedes. This affects at least 6,000 small-scale fisherfolk.

Tobias said in a statement that the planned wind project is only for the profit of foreign companies and its local partner.

The project reportedly started its pre-development phase in 2023 but the fisherfolk communities countered that they only learned about it in 2025.

It is just one of the three Offshore Wind Projects of the Copenhagen Infrastructure New Market Fund Corp. (CINMF), the first 100% foreign-owned company to be granted a wind energy service contract (WESC) by the Department of Energy (DOE). It acquired exclusive rights to explore and develop SMB for wind energy in electricity generation.

title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood as resistance vs US-Israel
content:
“We cannot condemn the genocide in Palestine without also condemning the imperialist United States.”

Filipino activists remembered the Operation Al-Aqsa Flood three years ago as the day Palestinians amplified their stand against imperialism.

Led by the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), activists marched on October 7 to the US Embassy to remember the historic operation against Israeli occupation after decades of Palestinian oppression.

Carrying the Palestinian flag and placards with images of slain journalists in Gaza, they marched along Kalaw Avenue in Ermita, Manila to condemn the Israeli attacks despite the ceasefire that supposedly took effect on October 10, 2025.

During the program, Amirah Lidasan, secretary-general of Moro Christian People’s Alliance and co-chairperson of Sandugo Movement of Moro and Indigenous Peoples for Self-Determination, said, “Gaza is not the land of another people. Gaza belongs to the Palestinians who are struggling.”

In 2025, US President Donald Trump introduced the Gaza peace plan, also known as the “Board of Peace,” which saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza. It also includes an agreement to end the war.

title: Palawan farmers remain landless
content:
FILE PHOTO: Women farmers in Lupang Ramos (Photo by Carlo Manalansan / Bulatlat)

CORON, Palawan — For more than a decade, 38 families of farmers in Coron, Palawan faced possible eviction from a disputed property awarded to beneficiaries whom peasant groups stressed are not the actual tillers.

The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) and Katipunan ng Samahan ng mga Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan (KASAMA-TK) said that the decades-long dispute over 887.76 hectares of agricultural land in Barangay Decalachao exposes the failure of agrarian reform programs.

The groups referred to the unresolved dispute involving the Philippine Agri-Business Center Corporation (PACECO) and the former Yulo King Ranch (YKR) where farmers organized under Alyansa ng Magsasaka at Mamamayan sa Yulo King Ranch (ALMMA-YKR) remain excluded from portions of the land they cultivate.

“From PD 27 to CARP, farmers have been promised land reform for decades, yet actual tillers remain excluded from the land they cultivate,” said Danilo Ramos, KMP chairperson, referring to Presidential Decree 27 and the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program.

According to KASAMA-TK, farmers began clearing and cultivating portions of the property in November 2009. The dispute affects 38 families or more than 200 people.

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Social media ban may exclude children instead of protecting them, advocates warn
content:
Child rights advocates have warned that a proposed social media ban could restrict children’s access to information, education, expression, and participation without addressing the perpetrators and platforms responsible for online abuse.




The warning followed the Senate’s approval of Senate Bill No. 2424, or the proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, on third and final reading on October 8.




The Senate approved the measure by a vote of 16-1, with no abstentions, advancing a proposal sponsored by Sen. Robinhood Padilla that would restrict minors’ access to digital services classified as high-risk.




Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns argued that the government must protect children from online exploitation, grooming, bullying, and other forms of digital harm without treating their access to digital spaces as the problem.




“Banning children from social media does not make the internet safe. It impedes children’s right to participation while the perpetrators remain,” said Teacher Elle Buntag, Salinlahi secretary general.




The group warned that restricting children’s access would not, by itself, establish whether platforms would respond more effectively to abuse or whether authorities would investigate and prosecute offenders more consistently.

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: On the Fringes | Days in a life as a daughter of a farmer
content:
When I was told that we were going to visit a peasant community in San Jose Del Monte, Bulacan, I spent an entire day preparing for the rural work. I slept early for almost a week trying to fix my body clock and walked for hours to condition my legs. 




We were required to bring boots, blankets, tumblers, tupperware, and our own utensils. We were oriented to eat what’s laid on the table and to not be choosy about where we would sleep. 




I did not expect that there would be host families that would allow strangers in their homes and feed them for three days. It was surprising because these families are not wealthy people. 




They are the ones who consider 5 a.m. as late for farm work and 9 pm. for a good night’s sleep. They are the ones guarding their crops and plants from landlords and business elites. They are the ones being displaced to make way for state-funded infrastructure. 




Yet, they are also the ones that would greet you with a contagious smile, a warm meal, and a welcoming home. Unlike the landlords, they believe that land is not something to be owned but to be nurtured, loved, and shared. 




True enough, I didn’t even need the things I brought. 




Our host family, Nanay Linda, guided us to the paths where we wouldn’t slip. She offered us pillows and blankets we comfortably slept on. She would buy ice and soft drinks, offer us coffee and chocolate drinks

title: Global day of action vs IMF-WB
content:
Photo courtesy of Asia Pacific Forum on Women Law and Development

We are really delegitimizing the IMF-WB.

BANGKOK – The People’s Global Campaign (PGC) against the International Monetary Fund and World Bank (IMF-WB) marked October 12 as the Global Day of Action against the two Bretton Woods institutions.

The Bretton Woods Institutions or the IMF-WB are financial institutions established in 1944 at a conference in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire in the United States. The goal was to establish a stable international economic system after the devastation of World War II. The IMF and World Bank have been criticized for imposing loan conditions that push governments to adopt liberalization policies, including deregulation and privatization.

In a press conference on October 12, representatives from the women, indigenous peoples, migrant workers as well as leaders in local organizations in Thailand spoke how the IMF-WB destroyed people’s lives through neoliberal policies implemented around the world.

“Today marks the start of the Annual Meetings of the IMF-WB, and for the next several days, behind closed doors, they will be deliberating on the next major neoliberal scheme as the world economy plummets into further crisis and the people slip into further destitution,” said Donna Denina, spokesperson from the PGC.

title: Groups decry military threats vs activist, media worker in Palawan
content:
Catagupan, Balabac, Palawan. Screengrab from Google Earth.

A network of alternative media organizations denounced the alleged intimidation experienced by a student leader and a media worker while conducting fieldwork at the Indigenous Molbog community in Barangay Catagupan, Balabac, Palawan.

In a statement, the People’s Alternative Media Network (Altermidya) stressed that no journalist or media worker should face intimidation, surveillance, or threats to life for doing their work. “These reported threats are grave and unacceptable.”

On October 8, Brent Sumague of the League of Filipino Students (LFS) Southern Tagalog and Marky Casaquite of Southern Tagalog Exposure, a member-organization of Altermidya, allegedly received threatening remarks from a certain Xyron Aliño who reportedly introduced himself as a personnel of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Western Command.

The two went to the area as part of a documentary they wanted to produce about the possible effects of Super El Niño on Indigenous peoples, as well as the impact of alleged land grabbing linked to the establishment of the military site in Balabac town under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between the Philippin

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: US intensifies sanctions vs. ICC
content:
Philippine-based and international human rights organizations condemned the sanctions imposed by the United States (US) against the International Criminal Court (ICC), citing adverse impacts to poor countries.

The US sanctions, declared on October 9 by State Secretary Marco Rubio, bans transactions with the court to paralyze its resources and its ability to operate. The sanctions impose legal, financial, and travel restrictions to certain individuals and institutions.

“The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes” said ICC President Tomoko Akane, urging state parties and the international community to stand against the obstruction of justice.

The administration of Donald Trump has previously sanctioned 13 prosecutors and judges of ICC, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese. The sanctions escalated after the ICC looked into war crimes committed by US troops in Afghanistan in 2018 up to the ongoing genocide of the US and Israel in Palestine.

author: Danilo Arao
title: Pagsusulit
content:
Woman writing in Baybayin/ photo from Nawaya

Nasa utak at puso pa rin ng maraming estudyante sa UP Diliman ang pagsisilbi sa bayan.

Sunod-sunod ang mga pagsusulit sa Unibersidad ng Pilipinas (UP) Diliman ngayon. Kalagitnaan na kasi ng semestre. Mabenta na naman ang mga bluebook na kadalasang ginagamit para sa eksaminasyon.

Bukod sa pagrerebyu, abala rin ang maraming estudyante sa pag-asikaso sa anumang backlog. May humihingi ng dagdag na palugit para sa papel na hindi pa nasusumite. May nakikiusap kung posible ba ang dagdag na gawain dahil sa mababang gradong nakuha sa ilang aktibidad. Siyempre’y may nagtatanong kung ilang beses na ba siyang lumiban sa klase (kahit alam na niya ang sagot).

Sa mahigit dalawang dekadang pagtuturo, mas mabilis nang nahihinuha ang mga nagsasabi ng totoo at ang mga nagpapalusot. Pero siyempre’y bawal maging mapanghusga.

Patuloy pa rin ang pagbibigay ng patas na desisyon batay sa personal na kalagayan ng estudyante. Sa panahon ngayon, hindi na uubra ang mga absolutong polisiyang may mabigat na parusa.

Kahit ang pagiging late sa klase lalo na sa umaga, minsa’y hinahayaan na lang. Apektado ng anarkiya sa lansangan ang mga estudyanteng gumagamit ng pampublikong transportasyon. At kung may sariling sasakyan, naiipit pa rin sa matinding trapik lalo na kung rush hour.

Totoong mas mabilis kung sasakay sa motorsiklo dahil nakakayang lumusot sa malilii

title: VP Sara impeachment: ‘It is now about how evidence will be used’
content:
A protester raises a placard with the message “Impeach Sara” during a protest in commemoration of Bonifacio Day on November 30, 2024. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

It has been more than 35 days since the commencement of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, and the prosecution panel continues to present evidence on the allegations faced by the second-highest official of the land.

For human rights lawyer and former Bayan Muna Rep. Carlos Zarate, however, the trial is no longer about confirming if there is clear evidence to convict Sara. The real fight, he stressed, is how the evidence could survive reconciliation, cross-examination, and constitutional scrutiny.

“That is where accountability can still disappear into the maze of all of this evidence,” he said during a roundtable discussion on Sara’s impeachment on Thursday, October 8. “There are now so many that either side can select the pieces most convenient to each narrative and story.”

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Fuel hikes squeeze jeepney drivers, commuters dry
content:
Jeepney with signage: "No to Oil Price Hike" (Photo by Roselle Ochobillo/Bulatlat)

By Wendyl Geronimo and Roselle Ochobillo

For commuters, the recent P1 increase in jeepney fares may seem small. But for workers who rely on public transportation every day, the additional peso can add to an already tightening budget.

For jeepney drivers, meanwhile, the bigger burden is not the fare increase itself but the fuel prices behind it.

After several rounds of oil price increases, diesel prices have continued to eat into drivers’ daily earnings, leaving some struggling to provide food, pay rent and keep their children in school.

The pressure was among the reasons transport groups, including the Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahang Tsuper at Opereytor Nationwide (PISTON), held a nationwide strike on Sept. 29 and 30, calling for lower petroleum prices and relief from fuel taxes.

For 52-year-old jeepney driver Teody Bermejo, National Capital Region and Alabang Pasay President said that the additional peso in fare does little to address what drivers actually spend to keep their vehicles running.

Bermejo, who has been driving for around 30 years, said he now spends much of his working day trying to recover the cost of diesel.

He drives from around 4:00 a.m. until 9:00 p.m., or as long as 16 hours a day. When diesel was around P50 to P55 ($0.80 to $0.88) per liter, he said he could take home arou

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Deterioration of civic space continues under Marcos Jr — global report
content:
Activists protest in front of Department of Justice to condemn the filing of twin terror laws against activists. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

MANILA — Civic space in the Philippines continues to deteriorate with the Philippine government’s failure to implement human rights obligations, global civil society alliance CIVICUS reported.

“Since coming to power, the (Ferdinand Marcos Jr.) government has sustained a systematic pattern of repression against activists, harassing those who defend human rights with the use of trumped-up charges or anti-terror laws,” said Josef Benedict, Asia researcher of CIVICUS.

The Philippines has been rated “Repressed” for five consecutive years — the second worst rating a country can receive — indicating severe restrictions to the freedoms of expression, peaceful assembly, and association.

The country was included in the Monitor Watchlist last March 2026, flagging serious concerns about its crackdown on dissent, criminalizing protesters, and targeting activists.

Read: Philippines on human rights watchlist due to crackdown on dissent

“The government must reverse course to protect the rights of activists and allow them to work without fear, interference or retaliation,” Benedict added.

Such a rating was a product of failure of the Philippine government to fulfill its human rights obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Po
